lede: From Chinon to the sentence of nullity. Each station names the passage it rests on; where none is carried yet, it says so.

stations.text: Jeanne, from Domrémy on the borders of Lorraine, comes to the court of Charles VII at Chinon and is examined by churchmen at Poitiers. (Modern accounts; module planned.)
At Poitiers, after her examination by the churchmen, Jeanne dictates a summons to the king of England, Bedford and the captains before Orléans: 'I am a chief of war.'
After dark, with the supply convoy brought in, Jeanne rides into the besieged city on a white horse beside the Bastard of Orléans, met with torches 'as if they saw God come down among them'.

Wounded by an arrow between shoulder and throat, she sends the captains back to the assault 'in God's name'; the Tourelles fall, and Glasdale and several hundred of his men are killed or drowned when the bridge, set on fire from below, gives way.

On a Sunday the English abandon their bastilles and draw up in battle; she forbids the French to attack on the holy day, and after an hour the English march off to Meung. The siege had lasted since 12 October 1428.
The English army is broken at Patay; Talbot is taken. (Modern accounts; module planned.)

Charles VII is crowned at Reims. The same day Jeanne writes to the duke of Burgundy, who had not answered her invitation to the coronation: make peace, and 'if it pleases you to make war, go against the Saracens'.
On the road to Paris she writes to Reims that the king has made a fortnight's truce with Burgundy, and that she is 'not content' with it and does not know if she will keep it.
The attack on Paris fails; Jeanne is wounded at the gate of Saint-Honoré. (Modern accounts; module planned.)
After the taking of Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier, a letter signed 'Jehanne' asks the town of Riom for powder, saltpetre, sulphur and crossbows; the siege of La Charité fails in December.

A letter in Jeanne's name, composed by a clerk, threatens the heretics of Bohemia with the sword unless they return to the Church. Quicherat's German text is dated at Sully, 3 March; a Latin text found since, 23 March.
In a sortie from Compiègne Jeanne is taken by the men of the Bastard of Wandonne, of the duke of Burgundy's party. (Modern accounts; module planned.)
The Luxembourg captor gives her up to the English for ten thousand livres; she is taken to Rouen. (Modern accounts; module planned.)

Pierre Cauchon, bishop of Beauvais, opens the proceedings at Rouen on 9 January; on 21 February Jeanne is brought before the court and refuses to swear to answer everything. (Module planned for the preliminaries.)

Six public sessions before forty and more assessors, then sessions in her cell: her voices, her sign to the king, men's clothing, the grace of God, and submission to the Church Militant. 'If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me there.'
The promoter's seventy articles are read to Jeanne; the judges reduce them to twelve propositions about 'a certain woman' and send them to the consultors.
The faculties of theology and decrees give their verdict on the articles: her revelations are lies or from devils, 'Belial, Satan and Behemoth'; she is schismatic and an apostate if she persists.

In the cemetery of Saint-Ouen, after a sermon and with the sentence half read, Jeanne submits, abjures in French and signs with a cross; she is sentenced to perpetual prison 'with the bread of sorrow and the water of affliction', and puts on women's clothes the same afternoon.

Found again in men's clothes, she says the promises made to her were not kept, that her voices told her she had damned herself to save her life, and that what she said at Saint-Ouen she said for fear of the fire.
In the Old Market of Rouen she is declared relapsed and heretic, cast out 'as a rotten limb' and left to the secular power, and burned the same day.
The duke of Burgundy makes peace with Charles VII. (Modern accounts; module planned.)
Charles VII enters Rouen; the next year he orders an inquiry into the trial. (Modern accounts; module planned.)
The papal commissioners declare the trial of 1431 null, void and of no effect. (Modern accounts; module planned.)
